query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.mechanism: Enhanced strain hardening due to the interaction between oxygen vacancies and dislocations, leading to increased uniform deformability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strain hardening and uniform deformability, resulting in increased strength and resistance to localization and impact-induced energy release.

generation.boundary: Strain rates ranging from 10^(-3) to 10^3 s^(-1) and temperatures up to 900°C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of oxygen vacancies required to achieve optimal strain hardening and uniform deformability is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Uniaxial compression tests at various strain rates and temperatures, with and without high-temperature annealing in a reducing atmosphere.

## Abstract
AbstractThe NbTiAlZrHfTaMoW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) system with the structure of the B2 matrix (antiphase domains) and antiphase domain boundaries was firstly developed. We conducted the mechanical properties of the RHEAs at 298 K, 1023 K, 1123 K, and 1223 K, as well as typical deformation characteristics. The RHEAs with low density (7.41~7.51 g/cm3) have excellent compressive-specific yield strength (σYS/ρ) at 1023 K (~131 MPa·cm3/g) and 1123 K (~104.2 MPa·cm3/g), respectively, which are far superior to most typical RHEAs. And, they still keep appropriate plastic deformability at room temperature (ε > 0.35). The superior specific yield strengths are mainly attributed to the solid solution strengthening induced by the Zr element. The formation of the dislocation slip bands with [111](101_) and [111](112_) directions and their interaction provide considerable plastic deformation capability. Meanwhile, dynamic recrystallization and dislocation annihilation accelerate the continuous softening after yielding at 1123 K.Keywords: refractory high-entropy alloys, B2 phase, specific yield strength, strain softening, deformation microstructure

To make these alloys more desirable for applications, including aeronautical engineering, automotive industry, and marine engineering, it is imperative to study their mechanical behavior as a function of strain‐rate. Hence, there has been an increasing interest in exploring the microstructural evolution and mechanical behavior of these MPEAs at high strain‐rates and temperatures.
